Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: Ana's eyes still widened at the sight of a kitchen knife, its sharp edge glinting in the fluorescent light. It was an ordinary object, one she used daily to chop vegetables for her family's dinner, but it transported her back to that night two years ago when her assailant had pressed a blade to her throat. The memory was fragmented, and Ana couldn't quite put the events in order - she recalled the feel of the cold metal, the sound of her own ragged breathing, but not the sequence of what happened next. When she tried to describe it to her husband or friends, words failed her, and she felt a familiar surge of rage. That night had left Ana with an unshakeable sense of vulnerability. She hated being naked, even in the shower or changing clothes - it made her feel exposed and defenseless all over again. Her husband's gentle touches now startled her, making her jump as if a stranger had invaded their bed. At night, when the house creaked and groaned around them, Ana's eyes would fly open, her heart racing with anticipation of some new threat. Even when her husband reassured her they were safe, she couldn't shake off the feeling that danger lurked just beyond the reach of their porch light. As time went on, Ana began to withdraw from her community work at a local non-profit organization. She had always found solace in helping others, but now every interaction felt like a reminder of her own weakness and failure to protect herself. Her assailant's words still echoed in her mind: "You should have stayed out of this." Ana couldn't help but agree - someone else would not have gotten into that situation; she had been foolish to trust the wrong person. She started to believe she didn't belong among her vibrant, strong Latinx community anymore. Ana's isolation only intensified when memories of the assault flooded back, unbidden and in chaotic flashes. Her mind replayed the sounds and sensations - the stench of sweat, the scrape of rough skin against hers - but never quite resolved into a coherent narrative. These disjointed recollections only reinforced her conviction that she was to blame for what happened; if only she had been more careful, more vigilant. When these memories surfaced, Ana would become convinced all over again that she couldn't trust anyone or anything - not even the lock on their front door. One evening, while walking home from work, Ana spotted a group of teenagers roughhousing in the park. The sight sent her heart racing; what if they were just like her assailant? She quickened her pace, eyes darting toward potential escape routes, and mentally rehearsed her defense strategies. But when she arrived at their front door, breathless and trembling, Ana realized that this hyper-vigilance was exhausting - she couldn't keep living in a constant state of high alert. Ana's husband noticed the change too; he encouraged her to seek help, reminding her that it wasn't weakness to ask for support. But Ana knew better: seeking therapy would be admitting defeat, acknowledging that she really was as fragile as everyone seemed to think. Yet something shifted within her when a close friend confided in Ana about their own struggles with PTSD - maybe, just maybe, asking for help wouldn't be surrendering but finally starting the fight back against this relentless cycle of fear and self-doubt. Ana's decision to seek therapy was motivated by the hope that she could break free from these suffocating patterns of thought and behavior. She knew it wouldn't be easy - the assault had left her with more than just physical scars - but for the first time in two years, Ana felt a glimmer of determination: she would confront this darkness head-on and reclaim her life, even if it meant facing those memories one last time.
